project.name: octoally
project.description: AI coding-session orchestration dashboard: a local Fastify + SQLite server with a React/xterm.js dashboard and an Electron tray app that launches, monitors and manages Claude Code and Codex sessions, agent sessions and terminals. This fork adds a native Windows port (winmux on ConPTY, Windows CLI and installer).

tour.title: What OctoAlly Is
tour.description: Start with README.md: OctoAlly is a local-first dashboard that launches, monitors and manages Claude Code and OpenAI Codex sessions from one web UI, built from three parts: a Fastify + SQLite server on localhost:42010, a React dashboard, and an Electron tray app. WINDOWS.md then explains what this fork adds: a native Windows port where winmux, a home-grown tmux replacement built on Windows' ConPTY terminal API, keeps sessions alive. Keep both documents in mind as the map for every step that follows.

tour.title: Server Entry Point
tour.description: server/src/index.ts is the single file everything hangs off: it has the highest fan-out in the graph and is the root of the dependency traversal. It enriches PATH so CLIs like claude and codex are found even when started from login, opens the database, registers every REST, WebSocket and tRPC route, enforces loopback/origin checks, serves the built dashboard and reconnects sessions that survived a restart. Two small Windows helpers run first: hide-windows.ts stops console windows from flashing when child processes start, and enrich-path.ts adds per-user tool folders to PATH.
tour.languageLesson: hide-windows.ts is a side-effect module: importing it changes global behavior (it monkey-patches child_process) without exporting anything you call. That is why it must be the very first import in every entry point, because ES module imports run in order before the rest of the file.

tour.title: Configuration and Database
tour.description: Directly under the entry point sit config.ts, which reads .env settings, migrates older ~/.openflow and ~/.hivecommand data into ~/.octoally and detects which terminal multiplexer is available, and db/index.ts, a better-sqlite3 singleton with ten files depending on it. The database holds projects, sessions, events, saved PTY output, settings and tasks, so nearly every later step reads or writes it. routes/settings.ts exposes the settings table and a getSetting helper that other modules reuse.
tour.languageLesson: better-sqlite3 is a synchronous SQLite driver: queries return values directly instead of Promises. For a single local process this is simpler and often faster than async drivers, because SQLite runs in-process and there is no network round trip to wait on.

tour.title: How a Session Launches
tour.description: When you start a Claude or Codex session, routes/sessions.ts receives the request and hands it to session-manager.ts, the core orchestrator. The manager forks one pty-worker.ts child process per session, so slow terminal work never blocks the Fastify event loop. The worker backs the session with tmux/dtach on Linux/macOS or the winmux daemon on Windows, using lib/pty.ts to load the right node-pty build (a PTY, or pseudo-terminal, is a fake terminal a program can run inside). session-env.ts strips the host Claude Code's own variables so launched sessions do not think they are children of another Claude.
tour.languageLesson: child_process.fork() starts a new Node process with a built-in IPC channel, so parent and child exchange JSON messages via process.send() and 'message' events. Here each session gets its own worker, isolating crashes and blocking native calls from the main server.

tour.title: Reading Session State
tour.description: Once a session runs, the server needs to know whether the AI is busy, idle or waiting for your input. session-state.ts works this out from quiet periods in the output, from a headless xterm in virtual-terminal.ts that turns screen redraws into readable text, and from Claude's .jsonl transcript files read incrementally by jsonl-reader.ts. routes/agent.ts builds on this so other programs can send input to a session and wait until it goes quiet.

tour.title: winmux: tmux for Windows
tour.description: Windows has no tmux, so this fork built winmux. daemon.ts is a long-lived per-user process that owns every Windows session's ConPTY plus a headless terminal mirror, so sessions survive server restarts and can be snapshotted. client.ts talks to it over a named pipe (a Windows inter-process channel) and starts it on demand, and protocol.ts defines the shared message format. This is what pty-worker.ts from Step 4 calls on Windows instead of tmux.
tour.languageLesson: protocol.ts uses newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON): each message is one JSON object followed by a newline. Stream sockets and pipes deliver arbitrary byte chunks, so a reader buffers data and splits on newlines to recover whole messages.

tour.title: Windows Commands and Paths
tour.description: Launching a CLI on Windows is fiddly, and these helpers absorb that. winmux/command.ts finds executables through PATH/PATHEXT, unwraps npm .cmd shims to call node directly and applies the different quoting rules of cmd and PowerShell. utils/platform.ts and xpath.ts give the rest of the server one way to handle paths (forward slashes, drive letters, containment checks), and win-shell.ts opens URLs, folders and Windows Terminal. cli.ts adds the `octoally mux` command for listing, attaching to and killing winmux sessions by hand.

tour.title: Live Streaming to the Browser
tour.description: Two WebSocket channels carry live data. routes/terminal.ts is a per-session socket: on first connect it spawns, adopts or reconnects the session at the browser's size, then relays keystrokes, resizes and output replay through the session manager from Step 4. routes/stream.ts pushes app-wide events from event-store.ts, which saves each event to SQLite and fans it out to subscribers. On the browser side, dashboard/src/lib/websocket.ts keeps that stream connected and refreshes cached session data when sessions start or end.
tour.languageLesson: event-store.ts follows the publish/subscribe pattern: producers call one publish function and any number of listeners get each event, without the producer knowing who is listening. This keeps routes like /stream decoupled from the code that creates events.

tour.title: Dashboard Bootstrap and Clients
tour.description: The dashboard starts at main.tsx, which mounts App.tsx; App wires the tRPC and React Query providers, connects the event stream from Step 8, sets up keyboard shortcuts and voice commands, and renders the home, project and Active Sessions tabs. All server calls go through lib/api.ts, the most depended-on file in the whole graph (21 dependents), or through lib/trpc.ts, which shares its types with the server's trpc/router.ts.
tour.languageLesson: tRPC gets end-to-end type safety without code generation: the dashboard imports only the TypeScript type of the server's AppRouter (import type), so the compiler checks every call's inputs and outputs while no server code ships to the browser.

tour.title: Project Workspace and Terminals
tour.description: This is the screen you spend most time in. ProjectView.tsx gives each project saved tabs for sessions, terminals, files, git and web pages, and SessionLauncher.tsx starts new Claude or Codex sessions. ActiveTerminals.tsx shows every running session as a draggable grid of cards. Each card is a Terminal.tsx, an xterm.js view joined to the terminal WebSocket from Step 8, with paste/drop of files and clickable file paths from terminal-file-links.ts.

tour.title: Files, Git and Previews
tour.description: Beside the terminals, each project has a file explorer and a git panel. FileExplorer.tsx and GitPanel.tsx in the dashboard call routes/files.ts (list, read, write, move, paste uploads, open in VS Code) and routes/git.ts, which wraps the git and gh command-line tools. preview-server.ts runs a separate loopback HTTP server on its own origin so HTML, images and PDFs can be previewed without getting access to the main dashboard.

tour.title: Claude Hooks and Status Line
tour.description: OctoAlly learns what Claude is doing through Claude Code's own hook system. routes/hooks.ts installs a hook into a project's .claude/settings.json. On Windows the hook is octoally-hook.cjs, which re-launches itself detached and posts each tool-use event to routes/events.ts so Claude is never slowed down. Those events land in the event store from Step 8 and show up in EventStream.tsx. statusline.cjs is the Windows Node version of the Claude status line, with no need for bash, jq or bc.

tour.title: Electron Desktop App
tour.description: The desktop app wraps the same dashboard in a window that minimizes to the tray. desktop-electron/src/main.ts creates the window, keeps the app to a single instance and watches the local server, restarting it if needed. server-manager.ts finds the CLI and Node (including the Windows install.json), starts and stops the server and checks port 42010. tray.ts builds the tray menu, and preload.ts exposes a small, safe API to the dashboard page.
tour.languageLesson: Electron splits code between a privileged main process (Node access) and sandboxed renderer pages. A preload script uses contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld to hand the page a narrow, explicit API instead of full Node access, which limits what a compromised page could do.

tour.title: Windows CLI and Installer
tour.description: This is how a Windows user gets OctoAlly running. install.cmd is a double-clickable wrapper around scripts/install.ps1, which checks prerequisites, builds the project, puts the CLI on PATH, writes ~/.octoally/install.json for the desktop app from Step 13 and optionally turns on start at login. bin/octoally.cmd finds node.exe and runs bin/octoally-win.mjs, the dependency-free Windows CLI for start/stop/status/logs that also forwards `mux` to the winmux CLI from Step 7. octoally-hidden.vbs starts it with no console window.
tour.languageLesson: PowerShell blocks unsigned scripts by default through its execution policy. A .cmd launcher that calls powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File install.ps1 lets users double-click the installer without changing their machine-wide policy.

tour.title: Testing, Release and Roadmap
tour.description: server/scripts/e2e-windows.mjs tests the whole Windows session stack against a real server on a spare port (42099) with a throwaway home folder: sessions surviving a restart, pop-out and re-adopt, adopting outside winmux sessions, image paste and shutdown. The GitHub Actions workflows release.yml and desktop-build.yml build the server/dashboard tarball and the Electron packages when a version tag is pushed. docs/TASKS.md is the Windows port's task ledger: what is done, what is in progress and what is next.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions workflows start from on: triggers such as a push of v* tags or workflow_dispatch for manual runs. Jobs run in parallel on separate runners unless linked with needs:, which is how a release job waits for the build jobs to finish and then collects their outputs.
